readerTitle: The two weeks you saved that changed nothing
caseNote: 가상 사례 (공장 포장 라인 설치, 앱 출시) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 프로젝트를 앞당기려면 모든 작업을 서두르는 대신, 서로 기다려야 하는 작업 사슬 중 가장 긴 사슬부터 찾아서 줄인다.
misconception: 어떤 작업이든 빨리 끝내면 프로젝트 전체가 그만큼 빨리 끝난다.

sources.text: Kelley, J. E. & Walker, M. R. (1959). Critical-Path Planning and Scheduling. Proceedings of the Eastern Joint Computer Conference.

factChecks.note: 포장 라인 계산: 기계 8 + 설치 2 + 시험 1 = 11주(주공정), 바닥 3 + 2 + 1 = 6주, 교육 4 + 시험 1 = 5주. 바닥 여유 11 − 6 = 5주, 교육 여유 11 − 5 = 6주. 특급 배송으로 기계 2주 단축 시 6 + 2 + 1 = 9주.
경로 이동 계산: 기계 2주 납품 시 2 + 2 + 1 = 5주, 바닥 사슬 6주가 가장 길어져 주공정이 됨.
앱 출시 계산: 디자인 2 + 개발 5 + 테스트 1 = 8주(마감과 동일). 개발이 6주로 늘면 9주. 법무 3주(여유 큼), 마케팅 페이지 2 + 2 = 4주. 기능 하나를 빼서 개발 5주로 되돌리면 8주.
주공정법이 1950년대 후반에 정립되었다는 내용은 Kelley & Walker(1959) 및 DuPont·Remington Rand의 공동 작업 기록으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 "late 1950s", "big industrial projects"로만 적었습니다.

cards.title: The two weeks you saved that changed nothing
body: A plant manager paid crews overtime to finish a new floor two weeks early. The new packing line still started on the same day. Not one hour sooner.
The crews did good work. The money just went to the wrong task.

image.label: Finished factory floor waiting, empty, for a machine
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 깔끔하게 완성된 공장 바닥 위에 기계 자리 표시만 있고 비어 있음. 한쪽 벽 달력에 개업일 동그라미, 멀리 트럭이 아직 오는 중. 실제 기업 로고 없음.

cards.title: You want the new line running sooner.
body: The machine takes 8 weeks to arrive. Floor and wiring take 3 weeks. Installing takes 2 weeks and needs both. Training operators takes 4 weeks. A 1-week test run comes last, after install and training.
Where should you spend to start sooner?

options.text: Pay overtime so the floor takes 1 week instead of 3
options.feedback: The floor would be ready long before the machine arrives. You pay extra and the start date doesn't move.

options.text: Pay for express shipping to get the machine 2 weeks sooner
options.feedback: The machine sits on the longest chain of waiting. Every week cut there comes off the finish date: 9 weeks instead of 11.

options.text: Do all three: express shipping, floor overtime and an extra trainer
options.feedback: You'd finish 2 weeks sooner, but only the shipping did that. The other two bills buy peace of mind, not time.

cards.title: Three chains, one finish date.
body: Add up each chain of tasks that must happen one after another.
cards.callout: The project can't finish before its longest chain does: **11 weeks**.

image.label: Three chains, one finish date.
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: The critical path
body: The **critical path** is the longest chain of tasks that each wait on the one before. Its length is the earliest the whole project can finish.
Every other task has **slack**: time it can slip without moving the end date. Here the floor has 5 weeks of slack. Training has 6.
Planners have used this idea since the late 1950s, when it was formalized for big industrial projects.

image.label: Task network with the longest chain highlighted
image.brief: 작업 네트워크 인포그래픽. 상자 "Machine 8w", "Floor 3w", "Training 4w", "Install 2w", "Test 1w"를 화살표로 연결. 기계→설치→시험 사슬만 굵은 주황색 선으로 강조, 나머지 사슬 옆에 "Slack 5w", "Slack 6w" 라벨.

cards.title: The critical path can move.
body: Now say a new supplier can deliver the machine in 2 weeks, not 8. The machine chain drops to 5 weeks.
Suddenly the floor chain, at 6 weeks, is the longest. The floor has become critical. The overtime that was useless before might now be worth paying for.
So after every speed-up, add the chains up again.

image.label: Highlight jumping from one chain to another
image.brief: 같은 작업 네트워크 두 장을 나란히. 왼쪽은 기계 사슬(11주) 강조, 오른쪽은 기계 상자가 "2w"로 줄고 바닥 사슬(6주)이 새로 강조됨. 가운데 화살표 "Path moved".

cards.title: Every deadline has a longest chain.
body: A restaurant opening waits on its slowest permit, not on how fast the walls get painted. A trade show booth waits on the printed banners if they take longest, not on the booking.
The question is always the same: which chain of tasks, done in order, takes the longest? **Effort anywhere else** feels productive but doesn't move the date.

cards.title: Slack is not spare time.
body: Paths are built on estimates. A task with one week of slack that slips two weeks becomes the new critical path.
Shared people break the math too. If the same electrician wires the floor and installs the machine, those jobs can't overlap, even if the chart says they can.
Watch the chains that are almost as long as the longest one.

cards.title: Now it's an app launch.
body: Your team ships a new app version in 8 weeks. Design (2 weeks) leads to building (5 weeks), then testing (1 week). Legal review of new terms takes 3 weeks. The marketing page takes 2 weeks after design.
Engineers now say building will take 6 weeks. What do you do?

options.text: Ask legal to rush its review
options.feedback: Legal finishes in week 3 and isn't needed until launch. Rushing it costs goodwill and saves no time.

options.text: Cut one lower-priority feature so the build fits in 5 weeks
options.feedback: Building is on the critical path, so a week saved there is a week saved at launch. You trade a feature for the date.

options.text: Add two new engineers to the build next week
options.feedback: Right place, uncertain result. New people need time to learn the code and can slow the team at first.

cards.title: Find the longest chain before you pay to go faster.
body: A project finishes when its longest chain of dependent tasks finishes. Speed anywhere else changes nothing about the date.
**Try it today:** pick one project with a deadline. List its tasks, note which must wait for which, and add up each chain. Which one sets your date?
